title: How Programs Execute: From Source to Silicon
objectives: Describe the pipeline from source code to running process: preprocess, compile, assemble, link, load
Trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle through registers, the ALU and memory for a simple statement
Explain what the linker and loader each do and what a symbol table is for
Relate compiled versus interpreted execution to the latency requirements of trading systems
motivation: You run the strategy binary and, microseconds later, the first order is on the wire. Between those two events, the compiler, assembler, linker and loader each did part of the work, and the CPU began a fetch-decode-execute loop it will run billions of times per second. Knowing that pipeline is what lets you read 'undefined reference' errors, understand what -O2 actually changes, and explain why the tick-to-trade path is compiled C++ while your research glue is Python.

blocks.text: From source text to executable bytes

blocks.md: A .cpp file is text - meaningful to humans, useless to a CPU. Turning it into a running program is a pipeline, and each stage is itself a program: the **preprocessor** performs textual transformations (expanding headers included with #include, and macros); the **compiler** translates the result into **assembly**, a human-readable mnemonic form of the machine's instructions; the **assembler** converts that into an **object file** - real machine code plus a **symbol table** naming its functions and variables, plus notes about which symbols it still needs; the **linker** merges object files and libraries, wiring every 'I need best_bid' to a concrete address; and the **loader** (part of the OS) maps the finished executable into memory when you run it.

blocks.title: What a build command actually does
items: Preprocess: headers are pasted in, macros expanded - one big translation unit.
Compile: C++ becomes assembly for the target CPU, optimised according to your -O level.
Assemble: assembly becomes machine code in an object file, with a symbol table.
Link: the object is joined with the standard library and any other objects; every undefined symbol must resolve or the build fails.
Load (at run time): the OS maps code and data segments into a fresh address space and jumps to the entry point.

blocks.code:
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -c engine.cpp     # compile + assemble: engine.o (not runnable yet)
nm engine.o | head -n 5              # peek at the symbol table
g++ engine.o feed.o -o engine        # link: resolve symbols across objects
./engine                             # the loader takes it from here
blocks.caption: Try it on any C++ file; nm shows names like 'T run_strategy' (T means a defined text symbol).

blocks.md: At run time the executable occupies a **process**: a private address space laid out in segments - **text** (the instructions, read-only), **data** (globals and statics), **heap** (grow-on-demand memory your allocator hands out) and **stack** (per-thread frames of locals and return addresses). The program counter steps through text; the ALU computes; registers hold hot values. This skeleton is the same for every process, which is why a debugger can always ask 'where am I?' and get a coherent answer.

blocks.caption: A process address space, top to bottom: the stack grows down, the heap grows up, text and data are fixed by the loader.

blocks.title: One statement's journey through the core
items: `x = 3 + 4;` compiles to roughly: put 3 in a register, add 4 to it, store the result at the address of x.
Fetch: the program counter points at the first instruction; it arrives in the core.
Decode: the control unit sees 'load immediate 3'. Execute: 3 lands in a register.
The add runs in the ALU in well under a nanosecond; the store writes memory.
At 3 GHz the whole statement costs a few nanoseconds - and the compiler may have folded it to a single constant before the CPU ever saw it.

blocks.md: **Ahead-of-time compiled** languages like C++ produce machine code before the program runs, so run time pays almost nothing for language machinery. **Interpreted** languages like Python compile to bytecode that a runtime program interprets: each source-level operation costs many native instructions of interpreter overhead. That is a fine trade for research, glue code and dashboards - and a bad one for a 50-microsecond tick-to-trade path. The desk pattern is hybrid: Python drives, C++ flies.

blocks.title: The budget in cycles
blocks.md: A 50-microsecond tick-to-trade budget is about 150,000 cycles at 3 GHz. Interpreter overhead of even 200 ns per Python-level operation means a path touching 25 such operations spends 5 microseconds - 10% of the budget - on language machinery alone. Which is why latency-critical paths are compiled, and why teams measure rather than guess.

The stages give error messages distinct flavours. **Compile errors** are about the text: syntax, unknown names, bad types. **Linker errors** are about missing wiring: 'undefined reference to quote_book::best_bid()' means some object used the symbol but none defined it - usually a missing .cpp, a forgotten library on the link line, or a signature mismatch. **Run-time crashes** come from the loaded program: a null pointer dereference faults because address 0 is never mapped. Knowing which stage complained cuts debugging time roughly in half.

guidedExercise.prompt: Your build fails with 'undefined reference to risk::check_limit(double)' although every header is included. (1) Which pipeline stage produced this error, and why can it not be a compile error? (2) Give two concrete causes. (3) What would you type to inspect which object files define the symbol?
hints: The compiler only sees one translation unit at a time.
nm lists the symbols an object file defines (T) or still needs (U).
guidedExercise.solution: (1) The linker - it is the only stage that sees across all objects, so a symbol declared in a header but defined nowhere fails here, not at compile time. (2) Likely causes: the .cpp defining risk::check_limit was never compiled or not passed to the link line, or its signature differs (e.g. an extra parameter). (3) Run nm -C on each object file and search for check_limit: 'T' means defined, 'U' means still unresolved.

independentExercise.prompt: Your handler executes 1,500 machine instructions per market message, averaging 1.2 cycles per instruction, on a 3 GHz core. (1) How many cycles per message? (2) What CPU time per message, in microseconds? (3) At 100,000 messages per second, what percentage of one core does the handler use?
hints: 3 GHz = 3 x 10^9 cycles per second; 1 microsecond = 3,000 cycles.
independentExercise.solution: (1) 1,500 x 1.2 = 1,800 cycles. (2) 1,800 / 3,000 = 0.6 microseconds per message. (3) 100,000 x 0.6 microseconds = 60,000 microseconds = 60 ms of CPU per second = 6% of one core. Even a 'fast' handler has headroom - which is why surprises usually come from cache misses and syscalls, not instruction counts.

commonMistakes: Assuming the program is compiled when you run it - compilation happened at build time; running is loading plus execution.
Confusing the linker (joins object files at build time) with the loader (maps the executable at run time).
Calling Python 'slow' without context: per-operation overhead matters on hot paths, not on glue code.
Ignoring optimisation flags: -O0 versus -O2 can change instruction counts by large factors on the same source.
realWorldApplication: Build systems, CI pipelines and deployment tooling all choreograph this pipeline; reading linker errors and understanding dynamic libraries is daily life for anyone shipping native services.
quantFinanceApplication: Tick-to-trade budgets are met by ahead-of-time compiled C++ on the hot path with Python tooling around it; knowing that the loader, not the compiler, runs at start-up explains why the first orders after a restart behave differently (cold caches, lazy binding).
summary: Source becomes a program through preprocess -> compile -> assemble -> link, with the loader mapping the result into memory at run time.
An object file is machine code plus a symbol table; the linker wires needed symbols to definitions or fails with 'undefined reference'.
A process's address space is text, data, heap and stack; the CPU runs fetch-decode-execute over text billions of times per second.
Compiled code pays language costs at build time; interpreted code pays them at run time - which is why hot trading paths are compiled.

quiz.prompt: Which stage runs immediately after the compiler produces assembly?
quiz.explanation: Assemble follows compile; the linker runs only after all objects exist, and the loader acts at run time.

quiz.prompt: 'undefined reference to foo()' is reported by:
quiz.explanation: Only the linker sees all objects together and can discover that no definition exists for a needed symbol.

quiz.prompt: How many CPU cycles do 1,500 instructions take at 1.2 cycles per instruction?
What does this C++ program print?
quiz.explanation: 0x04D2 = 4 x 256 + 13 x 16 + 2 = 1234 - the same bytes decoded in the binary lesson.

options: The loader maps the executable's segments into a new address space at run time
An object file contains a symbol table
The preprocessor executes #include directives by textual inclusion
The linker runs every time you start the program
quiz.explanation: The linker is a build-time tool; at run time it is the loader that acts (mapping any dynamic libraries). The other three are standard behaviour.

quiz.prompt: In one sentence, why is the tick-to-trade hot path compiled C++ rather than Python?
quiz.modelAnswer: Compiled C++ turns source into fixed machine code once, so run time pays nanoseconds per operation, while interpreted Python pays interpreter overhead on every operation - unaffordable inside a microsecond budget.
quiz.explanation: The lesson's budget arithmetic: 150,000 cycles is the whole budget, and interpreter overhead consumes it measurably.

flashcards.back: The assembler's output: machine code for one translation unit plus a symbol table and relocation notes - not runnable until linked.
Preprocess -> compile -> assemble -> link -> (at run time) load.
A named function or variable the linker matches between 'needed' (U) and 'defined' (T) entries in object files.
time = instructions x cycles-per-instruction / clock rate. Example: 1,800 cycles at 3 GHz = 0.6 microseconds.
